sections.section_title: Thessalonica -- Reasoning from the Scriptures in the Synagogue
sections.summary: Paul enters the Thessalonian synagogue and for three Sabbaths reasons from the scriptures, explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead and that 'this Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ'; some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks, and leading women are persuaded and join Paul and Silas.

sections.section_title: Jewish Opposition and the Charge of Another King
sections.summary: Jealous Jews form a mob, attack Jason's house, and drag Jason before the politarchs with the charge that the missionaries 'are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus' -- translating the messianic proclamation into the language of Roman treason; the politarchs take security bonds from Jason.

sections.section_title: Berea -- The Nobility of Examining the Scriptures
sections.summary: The Berean synagogue members are praised as 'more noble' because 'they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so'; many believe, including prominent Greek women and men, until Thessalonian Jews arrive and stir up the crowds, forcing Paul's departure to Athens.

sections.section_title: Athens -- Provoked by Idols, Reasoning in Every Setting
sections.summary: Paul's spirit is provoked by Athens's idols; he reasons in the synagogue with Jews and God-fearers, and daily in the marketplace with passersby; Epicurean and Stoic philosophers dismiss him as a 'babbler' or a 'preacher of foreign divinities' and bring him to the Areopagus to explain his teaching.

sections.section_title: The Areopagus Speech -- From the Unknown God to the Risen Judge
sections.summary: Paul argues from creation and the Athenians' own religious practice -- the altar 'To the unknown God' -- through God's self-sufficiency, the unity of the human race, the inadequacy of idols, and the call to universal repentance, concluding that God has fixed a day of judgment through a man he appointed, whose authority is certified by his resurrection from the dead.

The audience divides at the point of the resurrection: some mock, some defer ('We will hear you again about this'), and some believe -- including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris -- producing the smallest response of any city in Paul's journey.
